Capability blueprints show what an organization can do, and where the capability will be sourced from (i.e. future state). Capability blueprints do not show how an organization performs the capability, (i.e. take input X and produce output Y), or who is doing it. As a reminder, review how capabilities are a part of an organization in Strategy, Business Model, Operating Model, and Enterprise Architecture for more context.

The blueprints show the major groupings of capabilities for an organization to fulfil its mission, realize its purpose, and execute its business strategy. They are slightly different from capability maps in that blueprints also show the decisions about where a capability will be sourced from, or at times removed. These decisions are influenced by an organization's future state vision and design principles. Capability blueprints show the set of an organization's capabilities that will be:

  • Created (e.g. developed from scratch, acquired)
  • Modified (e.g. outsourced, automated, formed through partnerships / alliances), or
  • Removed (e.g. sold, decommissioned)

Ideally, the capability blueprint should be influenced by (or at have a mapping to) a generally accepted reference model (e.g. IT Capability Maturity Framework), or an industry standard model, (e.g. Supply Chain Operations Reference (SCOR) model). Having a way to map to a reference model can allow the organization to benchmark its capabilities (i.e. compare performance and costs to other organizations). If there isn't a known reference model, a process model could also be a good start.

To have documented decisions on the required capabilities that can assist in creating or making changes to capability maps, operating models or other supporting models that demonstrate key requirements to carry out the objectives of the organization.
